entries.title: US Fed raises key rate for first time in 3 years
entries.summary: In an attempt to address the persistently high inflation in the world's largest economy, the US Federal Reserve increased interest rates by 25 basis points. The president, on the other hand, said they should be cut.
entries.content:
September 16, 2026

In an attempt to address the persistently high inflation in the world's largest economy, the US Federal Reserve increased interest rates by 25 basis points. The president, on the other hand, said they should be cut.

The US Federal Reserve (Fed) on Wednesday raised interest rates by 25 basis points in an attempt to tackle stubbornly high inflation in the world's largest economy.

This move is sure to anger President Donald Trump, who has called for lower rates and who recently nominated Kevin Warsh to the post of Federal Reserve Chair.

"Our predominant focus is on the price stability side of our mandate. The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long," Warsh told a press conference.

Warsh has served as Fed Chair since May and during his confirmation process, he had assured Congress that central bank policymakers would "have no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation." 

"Today's policy action will support a ​timelier return to the committee's 2% goal," Warsh added.

The increase boosts the Fed's target rate to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%.

Trump had promised to lower prices in his 2024 election campaign, but things turned out differently after his inauguration. The US now faces the combined impact of Trump's global import tariffs, an energy shock following the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran, and capital spending from the artificial intelligence boom.

After the announcement of the rate increase, Trump said US interest rates should ‌be 1% or lower and that the rates ⁠should be cut fast.

White House spokesperson Kush Desai called the Fed's rate announcement "rather unfortunate," adding that Trump had been clear that he wanted lower interest rates.

Fed plans to 'stay in our lane'

Since his appointment to the job, speculation circulated around which direction Warsh would take the Fed, as Trump has pressured the institution to follow his lead.

But on Wednesday, Warsh joined the unanimous decision to raise interest rates, saying it had been made independent of what the market may be doing.

"We made this decision today based on our assessment of the situation," he said. "I'll observe market prices and see what they have to say. But today was our decision."

"Part of the independence of the Federal Reserve is we stay in our lane," Warsh said. "We let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane too. That's how we can stand up here and call them the way we see them."

Borrowers will feel some impact

The raise in interest rates will affect those who borrow money to make a large purchases, such as a home, car or large appliance.

The new rate will also raise monthly payments and costs for those who are already paying interest on credit card debt.

Currently, household debt payments are relatively low overall as a percentage of after-tax income. So many households will not feel the burden on borrowing in the short term.

But the move could be good for those who are saving, as interest rates on savings accounts and certificates of deposit will rise.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Germany: Oktoberfest beer prices rise, outpacing inflation
entries.summary: Oktoberfest's traditional beer mug, the Mass, will cost an average of €15.61 ($18.50) at this year's festival in Munich.
entries.content:
September 16, 2026

Oktoberfest's traditional beer mug, the Mass, will cost an average of €15.61 ($18.50) at this year's festival in Munich.

The price of a liter of beer at Munich's Oktoberfest has risen fivefold since 1985, far outpacing overall inflation in Germany, according to an analysis by UniCredit's chief economist in Germany.

A Mass, the traditional 1-liter (2.1-pint) serving at Oktoberfest, will cost an average of €15.61 ($18.50) this year. In 1985, it cost about 6.25 Deutschmarks, equivalent to €3.20 after conversion at the fixed euro exchange rate.

The figures were analyzed by UniCredit economist Andreas Rees ahead of the opening of the world's largest beer festival on Saturday.

Beer prices at Oktoberfest have increased by around 400% since 1985, according to Rees, using data from Munich's statistical office.

Consumer prices across Germany, by comparison, have risen by around 120% over the same period.

What determines the Mass' price?

This year's increase is considerably more modest. The average price of a Mass is up 2.4% from last year, below Germany's expected overall inflation rate of close to 3%.

"Beer prices at the Oktoberfest depend on a peculiar cocktail of harvests, energy prices, wages, tent costs, security and the willingness of millions of visitors to spend generously," Rees said.

Although the trend has been one of sharply rising prices, this year's Mass saw a price of 2.4% compared to 2025, the smallest increase in two decades.

Rees explained that ingredient prices could be playing a role, as hops have become cheaper while malting-barley prices have stabilized.

Festival draws millions

Oktoberfest is the largest folk festival in the world. Locals and tourists alike wear the traditional Bavarian lederhosen and dirndl dresses on the festival grounds.

The festival dates back to 1810, and it takes place at the Wiesn, a the local dialect abbreviation for Theresienwiese, the fairgrounds in Munich named in honor of Crown Princess Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen.

This Saturday, Munich will celebrate the 191st Oktoberfest, expecting somewhere between 6 and 7 million visitors.

The party begins when the city's mayor opens the first barrel in a ceremony officially marking the opening of the festival.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: UK: Village votes to 'secede' in asylum center plan protest
entries.summary: Residents of Piddington, a tiny, remote village in Oxfordshire in England, have staged a "referendum" on leaving the UK. They are objecting to plans to open an asylum reception center at a disused military base nearby.
entries.content:
United Kingdom

UK: Village votes to 'secede' in asylum center plan protest

September 16, 2026

Residents of Piddington, a tiny, remote village in Oxfordshire in England, have staged a "referendum" on leaving the UK. They are objecting to plans to open an asylum reception center at a disused military base nearby.

An English village of about 350 people has voted to "secede" from the United Kingdom, in a symbolic protest against government plans to set up an asylum reception center nearby. 

Residents of Piddington, about 25 kilometers (15 miles) northeast of Oxford, celebrated with a placard reading "Principality of Piddington" near the village road sign on Wednesday.

They oppose plans, still under review, to house asylum seekers in a disused military base, MoD Bicester (Site A).

What happened in the tongue-in-cheek breakaway vote?

The village's parish council said that 312 people cast ballots in the vote, a turnout of almost 92%.

Participants in the vote, which had no legal basis, were asked to agree or disagree with the statement: "I support Piddington seeking to secede from the United Kingdom and pursuing self-determination."

Of them, 285 voted to secede, 26 voted against, and one spoiled their ballot.

Parish council chair Tim McNally said that, going forward, the village would identify as the "Principality of Piddington."

"For us, it's about proportiality," McNally told Sky News. "How does a small village of 350 odd people assimilate with 1,250 males?"

He accused the government of "trying to rush this whole plan through."

An Oxfordshire County Council official told the BBC the plan risked making the village and the facility a "lightning rod" for potentially violent far-right protests.

The vote attracted the attention of self-styled anti-migration "influencers" online.

How did the government react?

The Labour government has been trying to move asylum seekers housed in hotels, an unpopular legacy they inherited from previous British governments, into disused military facilities by 2029.

This follows repeated protests at or near hotels and rented accommodation used for the purpose.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who only recently took over the rapidly rotating top job in British politics, promised to "look at the issues raised by the community and in the referendum."

But he also said that the "vast majority" of British people backed a government plan to stop housing asylum seekers in hotels and argued that it was "fair" to locate holding centers around the country.

Speaking to the BBC, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said a former military base was "a better option for housing asylum seekers" than hotels or rented accommodation.

One drawback with disused military bases, however, is that they are often intentionally placed in remote and rural areas. This can be ideal for military training and activity, but is less obviously suited to housing migrants with limited mobility and resources.

Migration and asylum have been contentious political issues in the UK for decades. But successive governments have faced particular pressure in recent years, with the populist right-wing Reform UK and Restore Britain parties gaining ground against the established political giants the Conservatives and Labour.

The most recent manifestation of this was anti-migrant protests in the coastal city of Portsmouth earlier this month. 

What does the government say about its plans for MoD Bicester?

In a Q+A published in July about its plans for Ministry of Defense (MoD) Bicester (Site A), the British government said the site "would provide basic, safe accommodation and would be designed to be largely self‑sufficient to minimize any impact on the local community."

It stressed the plan was still subject to feasibility studies, planning permission requirements and other red tape.

It didn't state how many people would be housed there, except to say: "The Home Office would take a phased approach to full occupancy, starting with smaller numbers at first."

It did specify that the facility would hold males aged 18-65.

The government said that if used, the site would be in operation for a minimum of 10 years. Relocating to military bases was "just the first step in the government’s work to exit hotels and source more appropriate accommodation to meet our statutory obligations," it said.

Safety for the local community, staff, and those accommodated on site would be "of the utmost importance," it said. The facility would be monitored round the clock by a security provider and via surveillance footage.

It would also be "designed to be as self-sufficient as possible including laundry facilities and communal spaces," the British government said.

entries.title: Chancellor Merz seeks CDU support as AfD encroaches
entries.summary: Following the CDU's crushing defeat in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, many are expressing doubts about the party's leader, Chancellor Friedrich Merz. But the CDU doesn't appear to have a viable alternative.
entries.content:
Germany

Chancellor Merz seeks CDU support as AfD encroaches

September 16, 2026

Following the CDU's crushing defeat in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, many are expressing doubts about the party's leader, Chancellor Friedrich Merz. But the CDU doesn't appear to have a viable alternative.

Earlier this week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was in Rovaniemi in northern Finland — nearly 1,800 kilometers (about 1,100 miles) north of Berlin — but even that wasn't far enough to escape the unrest brewing in the German capital. Representatives from various countries had gathered there for the European Arctic Summit to discuss natural resources, geopolitics, security and climate change.

When asked by journalists about the mood in Berlin, the chancellor said he could understand the heated debate in Germany surrounding him but that the future of Europe was far more urgent.

"That's why I'm trying to convince my friends, my political party, and my parliamentary caucus that this is important — much more important than some of the domestic political debates we're having," he said.

Merz was referring to the discussions and rumors circulating about whether he is still the right person for the job — not even a year and a half after he took office as German chancellor back in May 2025. That's because public support for the federal government has hit a record low, and the chancellor's party, the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), recently suffered a crushing defeat in the state election in Saxony-Anhalt.

Why is Merz so unpopular?

Another heavy defeat looks likely in the state election coming up in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. In the lead-up to voting on September 20, the chancellor's party is polling at a dramatically low 7%. Failure to clear the 5% hurdle to enter the state parliament even seems possible. Whatever happens, the CDU is likely to record its worst-ever results in a state election.

The election earlier this month in Saxony-Anhalt was won by the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which has been classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, the domestic intelligence agency, in this central German state.

Before taking office, Merz promised he would cut support for the AfD "in half." Instead, support for Merz's own party has dropped by half, and political circles in Berlin are asking: Is this Merz's fault? Is it perhaps due to his often abrasive communication style, or his failure to clearly explain important reforms — such as the one regarding the state pension system?

Members of the government are speaking openly about the lack of trust in the Merz cabinet. Education Minister Karin Prien (also of the CDU), for example, said on the public broadcaster ARD: "I believe that many people feel that the chancellor — and we in the CDU/CSU as well — lack the necessary empathy. And that has to change."

One frequently heard view is that Merz often comes across as lacking restraint. The planned pension reform, for example, would mean difficult cuts for many, but Merz often seems impatient when discussing it, commentators say. Back in July, the chancellor complained publicly that many citizens' attitudes about a "four-day workweek and work-life balance" could jeopardize the country's prosperity. Trade union representatives were outraged that the chancellor had accused Germans of being "lazy."

When the microphones and cameras are off, governing officials speak even more bluntly. The center-left Social Democrats (SPD), the CDU's junior coalition partner, are also sounding the alarm.

"You really get the impression that nerves are a bit frayed in the CDU right now," said SPD Parliamentary Secretary Dirk Wiese on the Welt TV channel. "I can only appeal once again to our coalition partner to really get back on track and work with us to do things better."

Two chancellor candidates: Söder and Wüst

But the problem remains that even if the CDU and its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), agree that Merz must step down as chancellor, there is no clear successor.

SU leader Markus Söder, the Bavarian state premier, has been named as a possible candidate. However, he often and readily provokes the CDU and therefore lacks broad support within the party.

Another candidate would be Hendrik Wüst, the CDU state premier of North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany's most populous state. Although he has quite capably led a coalition with the environmentalist Green Party for over four years, he has so far shown little inclination to move to Berlin. And most importantly, Wüst plans to run for reelection next April in North Rhine-Westphalia.

Provided there was enough support for a change of leadership in the governing coalition, there would be no major procedural challenges. Following the resignation of the chancellor, a successor is then appointed by parliamentary majority in the Bundestag.

However, if the sitting chancellor doesn't voluntarily step down, a "constructive vote of no confidence" is required. In this case, Wüst or Söder would have to openly challenge Merz — a scenario that no one can imagine at the moment.

Perhaps for this reason, too, all eight CDU state premiers declared in a joint statement on Wednesday that they still stood behind Merz. The statement reads: "People can trust that we will address their problems. As state premiers, we want to — and will — contribute to this effort together with the chancellor."

Germany needs "stability more than ever," the premiers said on Wednesday, calling for unity within the CDU and arguing that the way to rebuild voters' trust was through "listening and political action, not personnel debates."

The statement was signed by all eight premiers: Daniel Günther of Schleswig-Holstein, Boris Rhein of Hesse, Sven Schulze of Saxony-Anhalt, Kai Wegner of Berlin, Michael Kretschmer of Saxony, Gordon Schnieder of Rhineland-Palatinate, Mario Voigt of Thuringia and Wüst of North Rhine-Westphalia.

Pivotal state elections coming up

So while there isn't really a clear alternative to Merz, the chancellor also isn't someone who is likely to simply step down.

If rumors circulating in political circles in Berlin are to be believed, Merz wants to convene the executive committee of the CDU in Berlin as early as this coming Sunday evening, once the results of the state election in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania are in. His plan is to stand in front of this group of 22 leading conservative politicians and pose the question of whether his party is still willing to put its trust in him.

Merz's schedule for the coming week illustrates just how seriously he views the situation. The chancellor has canceled his trip to the United Nations General Assembly, an engagement that had been planned well in advance and was treated as a fixed appointment. "Contrary to the original plans, he will not travel to New York, as he is needed in Berlin," government sources have confirmed.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Can Canada and the EU build a deeper partnership?
entries.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Carney is known for standing up to US President Donald Trump. Now he wants to forge a "unique alliance" with Europe. But what could such a partnership look like?
entries.content:
Europe

Can Canada and the EU build a deeper partnership?

September 16, 2026

Canadian Prime Minister Carney is known for standing up to US President Donald Trump. Now he wants to forge a "unique alliance" with Europe. But what could such a partnership look like?

Before taking off for Europe, CanadianPrime Minister Mark Carney had set the tone for his visit, saying he was seeking to build a "unique alliance" with the EU. The Wall Street Journal similarly reported that Canada was considering becoming an "associate member" of the EU, while not aiming for full membership.

In her State of the European Union address on Wednesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen indicated that she was indeed open to such an expanded partnership.

"We believe that power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest, but to all of us," she said, addressing European lawmakers and Carney in Strasbourg, France. "That democracies have the freedom to choose with whom to work."

Von der Leyen said a EU-Canada partnership would cover a broad range of areas including advanced manufacturing, technology, defense production, the Arctic, energy, critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, cybersecurity and economic security.

Carney is expected to outline his vision for future relations between the EU and Canada during a speech at the European Parliament on Thursday.

What degree of collaboration could be possible between the EU and Canada?

EU member states are closely integrated economically, sharing a common market, trade and customs policy. When it comes to establishing ties with non-EU countries, a list of different options present themselves. They range from free trade agreements that scrap tariffs and trade barriers, to association agreements which may include political elements, to far-reaching economic arrangements such as participation in the common European market, as is the case for Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway.

The EU has already negotiated association agreements with Turkey, Israel and Ukraine. These have different objectives and may or may not mark a preliminary step toward full membership.

Patrick Leblond, an expert on international economic relations at the University of Ottawa, urges a little more caution around the term "association agreement." He considers it unlikely that Canada would adopt European laws or join the EU single market or customs union, which would mean imposing common external tariffs.

Leblond says Carney is likely more interested in forming a kind of alliance that deepens cooperation on issues of economic security and defense.

Closer defense cooperation?

"We have, in a way, taken the US [security] umbrella for granted on both sides. We have underinvested in our militaries," Leblond told DW.

He added that the focus was now on joining forces, for example in the production of military equipment and the development of new technologies.

Security analyst Anand Sundar of the European Council on Foreign Relations also sees great potential for European-Canadian cooperation when it comes to defense. Canada spends about 70% of its defense budget on US-made equipment, according to Sundar. Carney wants to change that, the analyst said, as it would pay off for Canadians to be part of European defense projects to get "more bang for their buck."

Canada has joined the EU's Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program. It provides EU member states with up to €150 billion ($173 billion, CA$ 241 billion) in loans for the joint procurement of military equipment. To qualify for funding, no more than 35% of the cost of the components can come from countries outside the EU, the European Economic Area (EEA) or Ukraine. Yet because Canada joined the SAFE program by paying a fee, more lenient procurement rules apply to its companies.

Nevertheless, Canadian companies still face significant hurdles for producing and purchasing weapons in partnership with European firms, Sundar told DW. The big question is how far the EU is willing to relax its own rules, the expert says, which could also have implications for non-EU countries, such as the United Kingdom or Norway.

'Underrated defense power'

"But the biggest draw for the European Union is really the fact that that Canada is an underrated defense power," Sundar told DW.

Canada, the expert added, spends more on defense than the 14 smallest EU member states combined.

The North American country invests 2% of its gross domestic product (GDP) on defense, Sundar said, with an increase expected in the coming years. Canada, like other NATO countries, has committed to spending a total of 5% of its GDP on defense by 2035, of which 3.5% will go towards military equipment and the remaining 1.5% towards other defense-related areas.

Protecting critical infrastructure

The EU and Canada also intend to discuss potential cooperation in the field of critical infrastructure expansion, such as the joint operation of space satellites or maintenance of fiber-optic cables in the North Atlantic, Leblond told DW. The goal here, too, is to become less dependent on the US and its companies. Moreover, Canada has oil and gas reserves that could meet some of the bloc's energy demands.

Trade relations between both have already been codified through the EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), which entered into force on a provisional basis in September 2017. The agreement eliminates nearly all tariffs between the EU and Canada, while also ensuring mutual market access for industrial goods, agricultural products and services. It even enables European companies to participate in public tenders in Canada.

Economic analyst Leblond, however, believes that CETA's potential has not yet been fully realized. He says many Canadian companies still tend to focus on the US and less on Europe. He believes it is the government's responsibility to provide more information about CETA and the opportunities it offers, saying the level of exchange envisaged in this format could also be intensified.

Why is Carney seeking closer ties with Europe?

In January, Carney delivered a speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos in which he warned of a "rupture in the world order," calling on the middle powers to act together.

"If we're not at the table, we're on the menu," he said.

Indeed, in recent weeks, the US-Canda trade war has continued escalating.

Even though it is clear that Canada cannot sever ties with the US, there is a growing belief inside Canada that the country needs additional allies, Leblond told DW. And the Europeans are considered trustworthy, he added.

Ultimately, the Canadians would want to see such an alliance, whatever form it may take, translate into concrete initiatives and projects through which Europeans and Canadians can help one another.

This article was translated from German

entries.title: Shock in Kosovo as Hague convicts former President Thaci
entries.summary: The conviction in The Hague of former President Hashim Thaci and three former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders has caused consternation in Kosovo — both among political leaders and on the streets. DW reports from Pristina.
entries.content:
September 16, 2026

The conviction in The Hague of former President Hashim Thaci and three former Kosovo Liberation Army leaders has caused consternation in Kosovo — both among political leaders and on the streets. DW reports from Pristina.

The announcement of the verdict was greeted with shock and profound disappointment in Pristina.

Thousands of citizens had gathered in the main square of Kosovo's capital, many waving flags of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA), to follow the announcement live on large screens. Similar gatherings took place across the country in Kosovo's main cities.

When it became clear that the Kosovo war crimes tribunal in The Hague had found former President Hashim Thaci guilty of war crimes — along with former Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) leaders Kadri Veseli, Jakup Krasniqi and Rexhep Selimi — the crowd fell silent.

The silence was followed by calls for justice and chants of support for the four men.

Groups of citizens began trying to demolish sections of the perimeter wall surrounding EULEX, the EU Rule of Law Mission in Kosovo, which was deployed in Kosovo after the country's declaration of independence from Serbia in 2008 and continues to operate to this day.

Large numbers of Kosovo police officers and special units intervened to prevent further damage and incidents.

Political leaders in Kosovo respond

It wasn't just the people on the streets who were disappointed: Kosovo's political leaders were quick to respond to the news from The Hague.

"The conviction of the former KLA leaders is a terrible judgment for Kosovo, for our liberation war," said Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca, who was present in the courtroom in The Hague when the verdict was announced. He called it "a major blow to the state and to the domestic narrative."

"Kosovo experienced the war itself. We know what the KLA war was about, and we know that there was no criminal mechanism to harm any population. It is a sad, unjust and undeserved decision," he said.

Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti called the verdict an "unacceptable injustice."

"The conviction and such a severe sentence for four former leaders of the Kosovo Liberation Army is an unacceptable injustice, a great and harmful punishment," Kurti said on Wednesday.

The Democratic Party of Kosovo (PDK), which was founded immediately after the war by Thaci and several other former KLA leaders, described the guilty verdict as an "unjust and unacceptable judgment," stressing that "the battle for justice continues until the very end."

"In The Hague, the right of our people, who fought for freedom, survival and liberation from the Serbian state regime that killed, expelled and terrorized Kosovo Albanians, was dealt a severe blow," the PDK said in a statement. "For us, this judgment represents a major injustice because it is based on allegations and material that we consider fabricated and which, over the years, have been promoted by the Serbian state apparatus and propaganda in an effort to criminalize the just war of the Kosovo Liberation Army."

The response from Kosovo's acting president, Albulena Haxhiu, was similar. She described the convictions of the four men as "a severe blow to their families, deeply shocking news for the Republic of Kosovo and a grave moment for the Albanian nation wherever it lives."

"On a day like this, the weight of this decision cannot be separated from the history from which we have emerged," Haxhiu wrote in her statement. "Kosovo experienced firsthand the violence of a state apparatus that killed civilians, committed massacres, expelled hundreds of thousands of Albanians from their homes and left behind thousands of people killed or missing. This experience is an indelible part of the memory of Kosovo and the Albanian nation."

Charges of crimes against humanity dismissed

The panel of judges at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in The Hague handed down the guilty verdicts over three years after the start of the trial and nearly six years after the four men were charged with war crimes and crimes against humanity during the 1998–99 Kosovo War.

Though the three-judge panel dismissed the charges of crimes against humanity, the four men were convicted of war crimes against civilians and political opponents who did not support the KLA during the war.

Thaci, who was indicted while serving as president of Kosovo, was sentenced to 25 years in prison. Jakup Krasniqi, who served as a KLA spokesman and later as speaker of Kosovo's parliament on several occasions, was also sentenced to 25 years in prison. Kadri Veseli, who headed the KLA intelligence service during the war, was sentenced to 18 years in prison, and Rexhep Selimi, who served as chief inspector of the KLA military police, was sentenced to 13 years in prison.

Defense lawyers for the men said they would appeal the verdict.

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers

The Kosovo Specialist Chambers, which was set up by the Kosovo Assembly (parliament) in 2015, is staffed by international judges and based in The Hague. It deals exclusively with cases relating to allegations of crimes committed by members of the KLA during the Kosovo War.

Before returning to join Kosovo's struggle for independence in 1998, Thaci had been a student in Switzerland.

As a political leader of the former KLA, he received support from Western leaders, who invited him to participate in the 1999 peace talks in Rambouillet, France. At the time, Thaci was seen in Kosovo as a leader who could guide the country toward independence.

About 13,000 civilians — most of them Kosovo Albanians — were killed, and more than 1 million people were displaced during the war, which saw Kosovo, at the time a Serbian province, fighting for independence.

Following NATO's intervention against Serbian forces and their withdrawal from Kosovo, Thaci founded his own political party and came to power, first as Kosovo's prime minister and later as president.

In 2008, Kosovo declared independence from Serbia, a move rejected and still not recognized by Belgrade, Moscow and Beijing. Kosovo's statehood is, however, recognized by over 100 countries.

Relations between Kosovo and Serbia remain tense after over 15 years of negotiations between the countries, mediated by the European Union and supported by the United States.

Thaci, who, like the other three men, denied the charges against him, resigned as president of Kosovo in 2020 to face the charges and defend himself in The Hague.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

entries.title: British-American writer Bonnie Greer dies aged 77
entries.summary: Chicago-born playwright Bonnie Greer, who became a familiar face in British political discourse later in life, has died. Her husband David Hutchins announced news of Greer's death.
entries.content:
United Kingdom

British-American writer Bonnie Greer dies aged 77

September 16, 2026

Chicago-born playwright Bonnie Greer, who became a familiar face in British political discourse later in life, has died. Her husband David Hutchins announced news of Greer's death.

Playwright and author Bonnie Greer died aged 77, her husband David Hutchins said on Wednesday in a statement to British media.

A celebrated writer born in Chicago who at first plied her trade in New York, Greer spent most of her adult life in the UK.

She took up dual citizenship and became a regular and prominent political commentator in Britain.

What did Greer's husband say about her death?

Greer's widower Hutchins hailed her as "an acclaimed playwright, author, critic, cultural and political commentator whose intelligence, courage and distinctive voice made an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life."

Hutchins said his late wife had suffered succumbed to a brief illness.

He said those closest to Greer would remember her warmth, humor, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together.

"To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her," Hutchins said. The pair married in 1993, seven years after Greer emigrated.

Who was Bonnie Greer?

Greer was born in Chicago in 1948, the eldest of seven children from a family of Mississippi sharecroppers.

Her familial exposure to the UK predated even her birth — her father Ben was stationed in Britain during World War II and had taken part in the D-Day landings. 

She gravitated towards creative writing amid the civil rights movement in the US after a college professor told her he did not believe women should pursue a legal career.

Having studied theater in Chicago she moved to New York as a young aspiring writer.

Greer settled in the UK in 1986 and worked mainly in theater with women and ethnic minorities.

She acquired British citizenship in 1997 and wrote a series of successful radio plays aired on the BBC and musicals. Her 1993 play "Munda Negra" exploring mental health problems among black women won the Verity Bargate Award for best play.

Greer also became a frequent contributor to political and social debate in Britain, frequently appearing on topical shows like "Newsnight" and "Question Time".

Greer was a prominent supporter of Barack Obama and wrote a memoir and personal musical history in 2009 called "Obama Music." She also campaigned against the UK's exit from the EU, Brexit, and Donald Trump's first term as US president at around the same time. 

She held a series of cultural roles, including being president of the Bronte Society, chancellor of Kingston upon Thames University in London, a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature, and a board member of the Royal Opera House and the London Film School.

entries.title: Gaza: At least 21 dead, including children, in building collapse
entries.summary: The search for survivors has been hampered by Israeli restrictions on heavy machinery in the Gaza Strip. Authorities say 2,000 damaged buildings in the territory are occupied by families who have nowhere else to go.
entries.content:
Palestinian Territories

Gaza: At least 21 dead in building collapse

September 16, 2026

The search for survivors has been hampered by Israeli restrictions on heavy machinery in the Gaza Strip. Authorities say 2,000 damaged buildings in the territory are occupied by families who have nowhere else to go.

At least 21 people, including six children, were killed in the Gaza Strip in the early hours of Wednesday morning when a war-damaged building collapsed, injuring at least 14 more people and trapping dozens of others beneath the rubble.

On Wednesday, rescue workers were still searching through the wreckage — in many cases with their bare hands given the lack of heavy machinery in the devastated Palestinian enclave.

"We are still hearing voices from under the rubble," said Raed Al-Dahshan, the director of Gaza City's civil defense service, adding that at least 10 families had lived in the collapsed building and expressing hope that more survivors could yet be found.

"My friend and neighbors live in this building," resident Mohannad Al-Mashharawi told the AFP news agency. "I came to help my friend retrieve some clothes and mattresses. He currently has no shelter or home."

The death toll is expected to rise as the search for victims buried in the rubble continues.

Gaza: Hundreds of buildings at risk of collapse

"The situation, you see, is tragic because we don't have the equipment and machinery that is needed," said Alessandro Mrakic, head of the United Nations (UN) Development Program's Gaza office. "So there are actually people ​are digging with their bare hands."

With wetter autumn and winter weather approaching, Mrakic warned that rain water could destabilize hundreds of other bombed-out buildings in the war-torn territory.

"There are approximately 400 buildings at risk of collapse," he said. "And we know that these buildings will collapse, especially now with the upcoming winter."

According to authorities, about 2,000 damaged buildings in Gaza are still inhabited by Palestinian families, many of whom have told the Reuters news agency that it is the only way to shelter from the wind and rain in the absence of sufficient tents.

"Today's tragedy underscores the grave risks faced by families living in these structures and the urgent need for safer alternatives," said Ramiz Alakbarov, UN Humanitarian ⁠Coordinator for ​the Occupied Palestinian Territory.

"No one should have to risk their life simply to find a safe place to shelter," he added.

Israeli restrictions on heavy machinery

Palestinian and UN officials have blamed Israel's restrictions on Gaza for the lack of heavy machinery available in the enclave.

Israel says it wants to keep such machines out of the hands of Hamas militants, who used such equipment in their deadly raid into Israel in October 2023, prompting Israel's devastating assault on Gaza which has since killed over 73,000 Palestinians — the vast majority of them civilians.

More than 1,300 Palestinians, also mostly civilians, have been killed in Gaza since a US-backed ceasefire in October 2025, while the Israeli military says four of its soldiers soldiers have been killed.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Forgotten US court of 'secrecy' could mean more deportations
entries.summary: The use of a secretive and long dormant court in the deportation of a woman from the US could have significant consequences. The Alien Terrorist Removal Court was just used for the first time in its 30-year history.
entries.content:
September 16, 2026

The use of a secretive and long dormant court in the deportation of a woman from the US could have significant consequences. The Alien Terrorist Removal Court was just used for the first time in its 30-year history.

An estimated 4.5 million people  have been deported from the US since 1996. But until this month, not one of those cases had involved the Alien Terrorist Removal Court (ATRC).

Nazira Haji Zada, 47, from Afghanistan, lived in Texas and had legal US permanent residency. According to a statment released by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) on Wednesday, she has now returned to Afghanistan after she "conceded she is an alien terrorist and waived appeal of the removal order, terminating her previous status." 

"This landmark case, resulting in the prompt removal of this alien terrorist to her country of origin, is a win for national security and the rule of law," said US Attorney General Todd Blanche.

However, Zada's public defenders Matthew Farley and Mary Manning Petras earlier said that the case "should not be seen as an endorsement of this court’s legitimacy."

The court, founded as part of a raft of anti-terror measures after the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing, was set up to deal with non-US citizens facing terrorism-related charges on which the evidence is confidential or somehow related to national security.

ATRC never needed before

Hiroshi Motomura, a law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), told DW that it appears the Donald Trump administration is using the ATRC as the latest tool in its deportation toolkit. 

"This is a very elaborate procedure. There are so many other ways that you can essentially get someone out of the United States by using the word terrorism in the context of removal proceedings," he said.

"From a very practical perspective, the government's non-use reflects its view over the last 30 years that 'we don't need this court because we can essentially deport people without it.'"

Zada was accused by prosecutors of being the "matriarch" of a family in which two men — son, Abdullah Haji Zada, and son-in-law, Nasir Ahmad Tawhed — had been found guilty of plotting to carry out a mass shooting on election day in 2024. Earlier this year, Blanche described the family as "ISIS-sympathizing."

For Motomura, who has written a number of books and teaches on immigration and citizenship, one of the key distinctions between the ATRC and regular means of deportation is that those on trial do not have a chance to view the evidence against them. Their lawyers may be able to in some cases.

Secrecy inherent in operation of ATRC

"I'm speculating, although I think not unreasonably, that this is someone against whom they cannot invoke terrorism or other grounds without the kind of disclosure in court that they would not want to have," Motomura said.

DHS said in the statement released on Wednesday that they provided Zada and her lawyers with "half a terabyte of documents," though it did not disclose what these showed.

"So they would rather go through a more elaborate procedure and disclose it in chambers to a judge as opposed to having it be potentially more public," Motomura said. "Because the procedure that this court provides is a procedure that calls for some disclosure, but also calls for some secrecy."

The ATRC consists of five federal trial court judges selected by the chief justice of the US Supreme Court, John Roberts, who was appointed by George W. Bush in 2005.

The government must first apply to the court demonstrating it has probable cause to suggest a person is an "alien terrorist" under the immigration law definition. It must also lay out why proceeding through standard deportation procedures would be a national security risk. In Zada's case this happened in July.

Then comes the hearing, in which the government need only prove their case "by the preponderance of the evidence", a lower bar than usually applied to such cases. Zada's decision to leave the country without the hearing means that the feasibility of the government using the court in future remains somewhat in the balance due to a constitutional point that was not tested.

Due process constitutional question yet to be resolved

"Dragging lawful permanent residents into court but refusing to show them or their attorneys the evidence that will be used against them is a plain violation of due process. We are confident that the Alien Terrorist Removal Court will be struck down as unconstitutional as soon as a judge is asked to address the issue," said Zada's lawyers in a statement to the Washington Post.

An amendment to the US constitution states that no state can "deprive any person of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law." Whether this applies in cases such as Zada's is not yet clear, something Motomura said may frustrate the Trump administration.

"I bet they were disappointed. I don't know this, but it would not surprise me if they're disappointed that the case never got litigated in court on the constitutional issue because it would allow them a different opportunity to limit the rights of people in the United States under the US Constitution," he said.

Given the Trump administration's stated "zero tolerance" policy on immigration — which has also included deporting people to so-called ‘third countries' they have no connection with and the widespread deployment of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents — it seems likely it won't be 30 years before another case is brought before the ATRC. And that could have significant implications for justice.

"I think it's very hard to view this situation accurately without seeing it as part of a broader effort by the administration to limit access to courts and to legal counsel and access to evidence on multiple fronts," concluded Motomura.

Edited by: Carla Bleiker

entries.title: After Neuer: Who will be Germany's new No. 1 goalkeeper?
entries.summary: Following Manuel Neuer's retirement, there are many candidates to succeed him, but which goalkeeper will Jürgen Klopp choose? What factors will play a role? And will Neuer's future have an indirect influence?
entries.content:
September 16, 2026

Following Manuel Neuer's retirement, there are many candidates to succeed him, but which goalkeeper will Jürgen Klopp choose? What factors will play a role? And will Neuer's future have an indirect influence?

Manuel Neuer retired from international duty after Germany's early exit from the 2026 World Cup, opening the door for a new No. 1.

Jonas Urbig appears the obvious choice, but Neuer is still the starter at Bayern Munich, which severely limits Urbig's playing time. If the 23-year-old was Bayern's first choice, he would likely be Germany's number one too. As it stands, though, it appears doubtful that Germany's new coach Jürgen Klopp will even call him up to his first squad. On September 17, he will announce his squad for four UEFA Nations League games against the Netherlands, Greece, and Serbia. And no position in the current Germany team is more up for grabs than goalkeeper.

Oliver Baumann: The automatic Neuer replacement?

Oliver Baumann represents exactly the kind of selfless No. 2 who could be the next No. 1. The Hoffenheim goalkeeper even commendably dealt with the humiliation of being replaced by Neuer just before the World Cup.

Klopp isn’t just tasked with celebrating short-term success with Germany, however. His remit is to bring about lasting change  making Germany favorites for a World Cup and a Euros once again. Oliver Baumann turned 36 this summer. The Bundesliga veteran will be 38 at the next Euros, 40 by the 2030 World Cup. His age might count against a sustainable rebirth of the Germany team.

The Hoffenheim goalkeeper, who has 13 caps, spoke to Bild in the days leading up to the squad announcement about his exchange with Klopp: "Yes, I was in contact with him. He'll say everything else on Thursday. We'll see about the rest—that’s for him to handle."

Ter Stegen: Back in Germany colors via Ajax?

Since Klopp prefers a highly attacking style of play in which all players press high up the field, he might opt for a goalkeeper who can also take on the duties of a field player. Marc-André ter Stegen would fit this profile better than Baumann. Ter Stegen is also two years younger than his competitor, though his career has been hampered by injuries.

After several serious injuries and a legal dispute with Barcelona, ter Stegen has gone on loan to Ajax, improving his chances of returning between the posts for Germany.

"As far as ter Stegen is concerned, I assume he’ll definitely be in the mix," Lothar Matthäus recently wrote for Sky. "If he continues to perform well in Amsterdam, he's a candidate for the number one spot."

Alexander Nübel: Out of the spotlight in Turkey

Alexander Nübel was Germany's third-string goalkeeper at the World Cup. He had been consistent at Stuttgart but moved to Besiktas this summer, where he has made a strong start. However, former national team goalkeeper Toni Schumacher sees the move as a disadvantage for the 29-year-old.

"His move to Turkey has taken him out of the spotlight," Schumacher, who also played for Fenerbahce for three years during his playing days, told Bild. "It simply has a positive effect when you play in your own country week after week and thrill the fans with your saves."

Loris Karius: History with Klopp at Liverpool

A goalkeeper who has never been called up to the Germany team but shares a history with Klopp is Loris Karius.

Karius, who has been at Schalke since January 2025, was at times Klopp’s No. 1 at Liverpool. However, he made two critical mistakes in the 2018 Champions League final against Real Madrid and was subsequently dropped.

Back in the Bundesliga aged 33, Karius is delivering consistent performances and may have played his way back into the spotlight.

"When people associate me with that, it's a testament to the performance I’m putting in. That's great," Karius said recently in an interview with Sky.

Keepers who could play for Germany or elsewhere

If none of the obvious candidates gets selected, there are a number of other good goalkeepers who might be considered. First among them is Noah Atubolu. The 24-year-old Eintracht Frankfurt keeper, who has Nigerian heritage, was the number one for Germany's U21s from 2022 to 2025, and was called up to the senior squad once last October.

Freiburg's Mio Backhaus is another promising talent. The 22-year-old’s mother is from Japan, meaning Backhaus is also eligible to play for Japan. He even played for the Japanese U15 team, but has since progressed through Germany's youth teams up to the U21 level.

In addition to Atubolu and Backhaus, there are also Augsburg's Finn Dahmen (28), Stuttgart's Dennis Seimen (20) and Diant Ramaj (24), who left recently relegated Heidenheim to join Copenhagen.

If Klopp wants to rely on one of the five, it might be worth playing them sooner rather than later in a competitive game. After all, just like Atubolu and Backhaus, the other three are also eligible to play for another country due to their heritage. Dahmen could also play for England, Seimen for Romania, and Ramaj for Kosovo.

Köpke: 'Develop a young goalkeeper as the No. 1'

"I think they need to develop a young goalkeeper as the No. 1 right now," Andreas Köpke, the goalkeeper on Germany's 1996 European championship team, told Bild.

Germany's former goalkeeping coach pointed to Bayern's backup goalkeeper, Urbig, alongside Backhaus and Atubolu — though only as and when Urbig plays regularly at club level.

And, given his standing at Bayern, that's bound to come down to how long Manuel Neuer chooses to continue to play.

This article was originally written in German.
